subject: bottlenose dolphin
title: Dolphins in Scotland Kill Porpoises, Then Leave Them Uneaten

scenes.text: Scotland's dolphins keep killing another animal. They never eat it.
Harbour porpoises, about four feet long, keep washing up on Scotland's east coast.
Ribs fractured. Spines shattered. Skin raked with evenly spaced tooth marks.
The marks match bottlenose dolphins. Where both live, dolphins cause about 64 percent of known porpoise deaths.
It isn't hunting, and it isn't about food. Fewer than 200 dolphins share the water with thousands of porpoises.
The leading guess: practice, for fighting or for attacks on young dolphins. The dolphin's smile hides a lot.

description:
Bottlenose dolphins off Scotland kill harbour porpoises and leave them uneaten.
Stranded porpoises show fractured ribs, shattered vertebrae and parallel rake marks that match bottlenose teeth. Where the two species overlap, these attacks account for about 64% of known porpoise deaths (Ross & Wilson 1996). With only 110 to 174 dolphins and thousands of porpoises, competition for food is unlikely; scientists have suggested practice fighting or rehearsal for attacks on young dolphins.
Did you think dolphins could be this violent?
first_comment: Similar attacks have since been recorded off California, carried out by male dolphins. Which animal has the most surprising dark side?
